title: A CXL Memory Rack for Multi-Turn LLM Serving
event_hint: HyMCache: a CXL memory rack for multi-turn LLM serving built from cost-efficient CXL-hybrid memory (CXL-HM: small in-device DRAM + large SSD-backed capacity behind a CXL interface), using request-level prefix prefetching and opportunistic write buffering to stage latency-critical KV reads in device DRAM; evaluated on a real CXL-HM prototype under single-aggregator (Llama-3.1-8B, LMSYS, 512 conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns) and PD-disaggregated serving.
problem: Long-context, multi-turn, and agentic LLM workloads increasingly reuse previously processed context, so KV-cache reuse is essential to cut redundant computation. But this reuse shifts the bottleneck to the memory tier that stores and serves reusable KV states at cluster scale: GPU HBM and host DRAM are too costly to scale to TB-scale shared context capacity, motivating remote tiers built from lower-cost, higher-capacity media. Conventional CMM-H devices treat internal DRAM as a transparent LRU cache, which mis-handles multi-turn KV access: LRU-induced refills let one-shot-wonder blocks occupy space that should hold upcoming prefix blocks, and dirty evictions interleave backend writebacks with read traffic, degrading effective read bandwidth. GPU prefix caching and LMCache local-CPU caching also lose effective reuse once the accumulated prefix working set exceeds their cache capacity (around Turn 3 for GPU prefix caching, around Turn 4 for LMCache local CPU in the single-node LMSYS run), because evicting an early block truncates the contiguous reusable prefix chain.
mechanism: HyMCache uses CXL-HM (small in-device DRAM + large SSD-backed capacity behind a CXL interface) as an explicitly managed staging space for KV objects rather than a transparent LRU cache. It exploits the read-dominant, predictable, append-only nature of multi-turn KV-cache access. Two design points: (1) KV-object prefetching — multi-turn prefix-cache lookup reveals the ordered list of KV objects an inference request will consume, and the serving runtime passes this object-level access order to CXL-HM via an explicit prefetch interface so upcoming KV objects are staged in device DRAM before foreground remote reads arrive; (2) latency-hiding staging window with opportunistic write buffering for newly generated KV. LLM workers access the remote KV tier as remote memory through RDMA (prototype path) or a CXL switch-based fabric; the remote tier is exposed as a unified memory address space backed by one or more CXL-HM devices. HyMCache uses an opportunistic remote-insertion policy: if the remote CXL-HM write buffer is full and cannot accept additional RDMA writes, it skips the insertion and retries in later turns rather than stalling the serving path, making it less sensitive to transfer-buffer pressure than distributed-DRAM Mooncake.

evidence.claim: Headline serving comparison with explicit DRAM budget (Section 1, PDF Page 2): with the SAME DRAM budget of 64 GB per worker (256 GB total), HyMCache improves serving performance over local LMCache by 3.0x in single-node serving and 1.45x in PD-disaggregated serving. Compared with 1 TB distributed-DRAM Mooncake, HyMCache trades a 30% performance gap for a 16x reduction in DRAM usage.
evidence.value: 3.0x vs LMCache (single-node); 1.45x vs LMCache (PD-disaggregated) at 64 GB/worker, 256 GB total; ~30% lower vs 1TB Mooncake at 16x less DRAM
evidence.baseline: local LMCache (64 GB/worker, 256 GB total same DRAM budget); 1 TB distributed-DRAM Mooncake
evidence.condition: real CXL-HM prototype, single-aggregator and PD-disaggregated serving
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 2 (Section 1 Introduction, paragraph following abstract)

evidence.claim: Single-node serving overall performance (Figure 11, Llama-3.1-8B, LMSYS, 512 multi-turn conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns, decode max tokens=1 to isolate prefix reuse): GPU prefix caching loses effective reuse around Turn 3 and LMCache local-CPU caching around Turn 4 (once accumulated prefix working set exceeds cache capacity, LRU evicts an early block and truncates the contiguous reusable prefix chain). HyMCache preserves reusable prefix KV blocks in the CXL-HM tier and maintains a cache hit rate close to 90% across turns, avoiding the recomputation-driven latency growth that drives baselines back toward the recomputation curve.
evidence.value: HyMCache ~90% cache hit rate across turns; GPU prefix caching loses reuse ~Turn 3; LMCache local CPU ~Turn 4
evidence.baseline: Recomputation; GPU Prefix Caching (T1); LMCache (T1 + local DRAM)
evidence.condition: Llama-3.1-8B, LMSYS, 512 conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns, decode max=1

evidence.claim: Transfer-buffer sensitivity vs distributed-DRAM Mooncake (Figure 10, Section 6.2 narrative): with the same 10 GB of additional host DRAM per node as a transfer buffer, Mooncake suffers severe transfer-buffer pressure — many remote KV insertions fail to complete in time, lowering effective KV reuse and breaking the contiguous prefix chain in later turns, so performance approaches the recomputation baseline even with a longer transfer timeout. HyMCache is less sensitive (its opportunistic remote-insertion policy skips and retries rather than stalling) and shows similar performance beyond a 10 GB transfer-buffer budget; Mooncake recovers only as the transfer-buffer budget increases.
evidence.value: Mooncake approaches recomputation at 10 GB transfer buffer; HyMCache insensitive beyond 10 GB
evidence.condition: varying per-node transfer-buffer host DRAM budget; same 10 GB/node starting point

evidence.claim: Prefetching microbenchmark (Figure 13a): on heavy random-read requests to the remote CXL-HM tier managed by HyMCache, enabling prefetching improves performance by 37% vs prefetch-off.
evidence.condition: heavy random-read microbenchmark against remote CXL-HM tier

evidence.claim: Workload motivation (Section 3): multi-turn KV-cache access is read-dominant, predictable, and append-only; conventional CMM-H LRU management mis-handles it — LRU refills leave one-shot-wonder blocks occupying space needed for upcoming prefix blocks, and dirty evictions interleave backend writebacks with reads, degrading effective read bandwidth. This motivates treating CXL-HM internal DRAM as an explicitly managed staging space rather than a transparent cache. KV-cache tiers framed via NVIDIA's G1-G4 hierarchy (G1 GPU HBM, G2 system DRAM via LMCache/Mooncake, G3 local SSD, G4 shared remote storage via NVMe-oF/RDMA/DPU).
evidence.value: multi-turn KV access read-dominant/predictable/append-only; LRU + dirty eviction degrade CMM-H read bandwidth; G1-G4 tier framing
evidence.condition: multi-turn LLM serving KV-cache access pattern analysis

evaluation_context: Hardware: a real CXL-HM prototype (small in-device DRAM + large SSD-backed capacity behind a CXL interface); remote KV tier accessed as remote memory via RDMA (prototype example path) or CXL switch-based fabric; one or more CXL-HM devices forming a unified address space. DRAM budget for the LMCache comparison: 64 GB per worker, 256 GB total, held equal. Mooncake comparator: 1 TB distributed-DRAM, with a per-node transfer-buffer host-DRAM budget varied (10 GB starting point). Single-node serving workload: Llama-3.1-8B on LMSYS dataset, 512 multi-turn conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns, decode max tokens=1 to isolate prefix reuse and prefill-side latency. Baselines: Recomputation, GPU Prefix Caching (T1), LMCache (T1 + local DRAM), Redis-only (T1 + Redis 64 GB), LMCache + Redis (T1 + local 64 GB + Redis 64 GB), and 1 TB distributed-DRAM Mooncake. Prefetch microbenchmark: heavy random reads against the remote CXL-HM tier. KV-cache tiering framed via NVIDIA G1-G4 hierarchy.
limitations: The supplement confirms the DRAM budget (64 GB/worker, 256 GB total) behind the 3.0x/1.45x vs LMCache headline, the Mooncake config (1 TB distributed DRAM), and the single-node workload (Llama-3.1-8B, LMSYS, 512 conversations, concurrency 32, up to 10 turns, decode max=1). However, the absolute per-config throughput (tokens/s or req/s) and absolute P99 TTFT/P99 E2E latency values are still only available as Figure 11/12 axis ranges and curves, not as a per-turn numeric table, so the precise per-turn magnitudes behind the 3.0x/1.45x ratios are read off the figures. The single-node serving workload caps decode tokens at 1 to isolate prefix reuse, so the result does not directly represent decode-heavy or agentic multi-tool workloads. Prototype uses RDMA as the example access path; the CXL switch-fabric variant is described but its separate measurements are not in the visible evidence. Absolute CXL-HM device DRAM/SSD capacities, device count, and SSD media type (TLC/QLC) are not pinned in the visible evidence. Single-prototype scope; no multi-rack, concurrency-scaling beyond 32/64, or failure-mode evaluation is visible. The PD-disaggregated serving absolute numbers (vs only the LMCache baseline at the same DRAM budget) are less exposed than the single-node figures.
project_relevance: Relevant to the cross-region / Agent-Cache card's question of how to store, move, and reuse KV-cache (and by extension reusable agent context) at cluster scale using lower-cost, higher-capacity media: HyMCache is a concrete CXL-HM rack that treats device DRAM as an explicitly managed staging space for predictable, append-only multi-turn KV access, using request-level prefix prefetching to hide SSD latency. The now-confirmed 16x-DRAM-reduction vs 1 TB Mooncake at a 30% performance cost (and 3.0x/1.45x over LMCache at equal 64 GB/worker DRAM budget) is a directly relevant cost/capacity tradeoff point for TB-scale shared context. The transfer-buffer sensitivity finding (distributed-DRAM Mooncake needs substantial extra local host DRAM as a transfer buffer, while HyMCache's opportunistic insertion is insensitive) is a concrete data-point on the consistency/buffering overhead the card asks about. The prefetching design (object-level access order revealed by prefix-cache lookup, passed to the device) is a concrete instance of the card's 'prefetch and placement to reduce latency' lever. Caveat: the result is single-turn-reuse KV (decode capped at 1) rather than WAN cross-region, so it speaks to shared-tier capacity more than to WAN RTT tradeoffs.
